clue.text: Saucy line penned by dandy for coquette

parts.note: flip is an informal word for flippant or pert

indicators.note: something penned by a person is enclosed by them, as a pen holds sheep

parts.note: a fop is a vain, overdressed man
L is the standard abbreviation for line

explanation.surface: A dandy writes a cheeky line to win over a flirtatious young woman.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the weakest link here: a flip-flop is someone who keeps changing sides, as a coquette does with admirers.
explanation.definitionFit: A coquette plays one admirer off against another, and a flip-flop is a person who keeps reversing position.

clue.text: Runs in hand give time

indicators.note: in places one piece inside the other

parts.note: a fist is a closed hand
R is the cricket abbreviation for runs

explanation.surface: A cricket captain with runs in hand can afford to give the batsmen time.
explanation.walkthrough: R goes inside FIST. Frist is an old and dialect word, chiefly Scots.
explanation.definitionFit: To frist is to grant a delay, especially extra time to pay a debt, which is giving someone time.

clue.text: Decorative light? Electrical unit's grabbed by cat

indicators.note: something grabbed is held tight, so one piece is clutched inside the other

parts.note: a lion is a big cat
the amp is the unit of electric current

explanation.surface: A cat pounces on a fairy light and grabs its plug.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cat' could be any feline; it has to be the big cat whose name can hold the unit.
explanation.definitionFit: A lampion is a small oil lamp, often of coloured glass, used in festive illuminations.

clue.text: Fabulous bird, gamine almost excessively posh?

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the next word loses its final letter

parts.note: a gamine is an impish, mischievous girl, so an imp
unduly means to an excessive degree
U means upper-class, the posh usage

explanation.surface: A boyish young woman is called a fabulous bird, a little too posh.
explanation.walkthrough: IMP, then UNDULY without its last letter, then U. The question mark marks the surface's joke of 'bird' as a girl.
explanation.definitionFit: The impundulu is the lightning bird of southern African folklore, a legendary creature rather than a real one.

clue.text: Fastin' dispelled impure spirit

indicators.note: something dispelled is driven off and scattered, so the letters are reordered

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged, the apostrophe ignored

explanation.surface: Fasting drives out an evil spirit, as in an exorcism.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Impure spirit' sounds like a demon; it is distilling.
explanation.definitionFit: Faints, also spelt feints, are the impure liquor that comes off first and last in whisky distillation.

clue.text: Fan of the Algarve perhaps, soul I help in trouble

indicators.note: letters in trouble are in disarray, so they are rearranged

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A holidaymaker who loves southern Portugal offers to help some poor soul in difficulty.
explanation.walkthrough: The Algarve is the southern coast of Portugal, so 'perhaps' marks it as one example of what is loved.
explanation.definitionFit: A Lusophile admires Portugal and its culture; someone who loves the Algarve is one example.

clue.text: Second to last in lots of amyl group

indicators.note: the second letter is lifted out of its place and sent to the end of the word

parts.note: plenty means lots

explanation.surface: A chemist puts the second-to-last test tube among lots of amyl compounds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Second to last' looks like the penultimate; here it says move the second letter to the end of PLENTY.
explanation.definitionFit: Pentyl is the systematic chemical name for the five-carbon amyl group.

clue.text: Group inside furled umbrellas without a sound

indicators.note: a group of letters sitting inside the words that follow, running across their join

parts.note: the run of letters straddling the two words

explanation.surface: A party of walkers sheltering under rolled-up umbrellas, saying nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Group' looks like the people under the umbrellas, but it only marks a cluster of letters lying inside the next two words.
explanation.definitionFit: Dumb means unable or unwilling to speak, so making no sound at all.

clue.text: Unenthusiastic restraint put on pedal

indicators.note: put on in a down answer means placed above, so the first piece sits before the second

parts.note: a dam restrains water
P is taken from pedal; its exact justification is uncertain

explanation.surface: Someone half-heartedly rides a bike with the brake on.
explanation.walkthrough: DAM followed by P. The P from 'pedal' is not fully explained.
explanation.definitionFit: Damp can mean lacking spirit or enthusiasm, as in a damp squib or a damp response.

clue.text: Unit advanced in battle

indicators.note: in places one piece inside the other

parts.note: Mons in Belgium saw a famous First World War battle
A is an abbreviation for advanced

explanation.surface: An army unit pushed forward during a battle.
explanation.walkthrough: A goes inside MONS. 'Unit' looks military; it is the philosophical sense.
explanation.definitionFit: A monas, or monad, is an ultimate indivisible unit, as in philosophy or biology.

clue.text: Mean, old, retaining puff in climbing peak

indicators.note: retaining means holding on to, so one piece is kept inside the other
climbing in a down answer reads upwards, so the word is turned around

parts.note: a neb is a beak or pointed tip
a toke is a puff on a cigarette or joint

explanation.surface: A miserly old man keeps puffing away as he climbs a mountain.
explanation.walkthrough: TOKE goes inside BEN. The role of 'old' is not fully clear; it may just paint the surface's old man.
explanation.definitionFit: To betoken is to signify or indicate, which is what to mean something is.

clue.text: Storm in the Cairngorms? Argue furiously about faulty map

indicators.note: about means around, so one scrambled group goes round the other
doing something furiously throws it into disorder, so the letters before it are scrambled

parts.note: the first set of letters to be scrambled

indicators.note: something faulty is not in working order, so the following letters need rearranging

parts.note: the second set of letters to be scrambled

explanation.surface: A furious row breaks out on a Highland walk over a map that has led everyone astray.
explanation.walkthrough: RAUGE is wrapped around AMP to give RAMPAUGE. The Cairngorms are Scottish mountains, so the question mark points to a Scots word.
explanation.definitionFit: Rampauge is the Scots form of rampage, to rush about violently, which is what storming means.

clue.text: Bail money gets characters released regularly — it's bitter to swallow

indicators.note: letters let go at regular intervals leave only every other letter of the phrase behind

parts.note: the second, fourth, sixth and eighth letters of the two words

explanation.surface: Someone pays out bail money only to see the prisoners freed again, a hard thing to accept.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Released' and 'bail' both suggest prisoners going free, but the characters released are letters dropped from 'Bail money'.
explanation.definitionFit: Aloe is a famously bitter purgative drug taken from the plant's leaves, hard to swallow in the literal sense.

clue.text: Irons being hammered on chaps, in past?

definitions.text: Irons being hammered on chaps, in past?

indicators.note: in tells us the pieces so far sit inside the abbreviation that follows

parts.note: PT is the grammar abbreviation for past tense

indicators.note: on means placed next to, so one piece follows directly after the other
metal being hammered is beaten into a new shape, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged
chaps are men

explanation.surface: Leg irons hammered onto men's ankles in an earlier age.
explanation.walkthrough: Read whole, the clue also describes the thing: men fettered in irons in the past, and the word itself is an old one.
explanation.definitionFit: Prisonment is an archaic word for imprisonment, the state of men clapped in irons in former times.

clue.text: Reject hurtled, bagging runs

indicators.note: bagging something means putting it in a bag, so one piece is held inside another

parts.note: spun can mean sped along, as a car spins down a road
R is the cricket abbreviation for runs

explanation.surface: A rejected bowler storms off, having conceded plenty of runs.
explanation.walkthrough: R goes inside SPUN to give SPURN.
explanation.definitionFit: To spurn is to reject with contempt, a direct synonym used as a verb.

clue.text: Lily seeds according to art restricting a painful ailment

indicators.note: restricting means hemming in, so the abbreviation wraps around the rest

parts.note: S.A. abbreviates secundum artem, Latin for according to art, a pharmacists' term
taken as written
a bad back is a painful one
an ill is an ailment

explanation.surface: A herbalist prescribes lily seeds, by the book, to treat a painful complaint.
explanation.walkthrough: 'According to art' is a prescription formula from old pharmacy Latin, which is why it gives just two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Sabadilla is the seed of a Mexican plant of the lily family, used as an insecticide and in medicine.

clue.text: What can make you little more than this, when done for- Cremating

definitions.text: What can make you little more than this, when done for- Cremating

indicators.note: done for means ruined or wrecked, so the word after it is broken up and rearranged

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A grim reflection that once you are dead and burnt, very little of you remains.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition: cremation reduces a body to a tiny weight of ash, and the word CREMATING rearranges into that weight.
explanation.definitionFit: A centigram is a hundredth of a gram, a tiny weight, an exaggeration of how little cremation leaves.

clue.text: Number kept in touch, giving a ring

indicators.note: something kept in another thing is held inside it

parts.note: tig is the playground game of tag, in which players touch each other
N is the abbreviation for number

explanation.surface: A phone number kept handy so a friend can give you a ring.
explanation.walkthrough: N goes inside TIG to give TING. 'Ring' here is a sound, not a phone call.
explanation.definitionFit: A ting is a single clear ringing sound, as of a small bell being struck.

clue.text: Check-out area possibly exercising keypads

indicators.note: exercising works things over, and possibly says the result may take another form, so the letters move

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: At the supermarket till, the cashier is busy tapping away on keypads.
explanation.definitionFit: A pay desk is the counter where customers settle their bills, which is what a check-out is.

clue.text: 'Airy area in drain? Poker required (7, two words)

indicators.note: in places one piece inside the other

parts.note: to suck something dry is to drain it
a head is a hairy area, and the apostrophe drops its H as a Cockney would

explanation.surface: Someone asks for a poker to clear a blocked drain in a hairy spot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Poker' looks like the fireside tool; it is a dialect name for the pochard, a diving duck.
explanation.definitionFit: The pochard, called a poker in dialect, is a diving duck of the kind grouped loosely with sea ducks.

clue.text: Bowled with old Shane spinning ''round'': very fair

indicators.note: round means surrounding, so the scrambled letters go about the single letter
a spinning thing is whirled about, so these letters are thrown into a new order

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged
B is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for bowled

explanation.surface: A batsman is bowled by the veteran leg-spinner Shane Warne, and the umpire rules it entirely fair.
explanation.walkthrough: Shane Warne was a famous Australian spin bowler, which makes 'old' look like a description, but it is part of the letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Ash blonde is a very pale, greyish shade of fair hair, so the phrase describes someone extremely fair.

clue.text: Plague endlessly worried magistracy of old

indicators.note: endlessly means without an end, so the last letter is dropped

parts.note: to dog someone is to plague or pursue them
eaten, as in eaten up with worry, means worried

explanation.surface: An old magistrate's office is beset by endless anxieties.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plague' looks like the disease; it is the verb, to pester.
explanation.definitionFit: A dogeate is the office or term of a doge, the chief magistrate of old Venice or Genoa.

clue.text: Articulate hook-like parts, growing out at edges

indicators.note: a word placed at the edges sits on both sides, wrapping what lies between

parts.note: enate is a botanical term for growing out from something
unci is the plural of uncus, a hooked structure in anatomy

explanation.surface: A naturalist describes jointed hooked limbs sprouting out along the margins.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Articulate' sounds like a jointed body part beside 'hook-like parts', but it is the verb meaning to speak clearly.
explanation.definitionFit: To enunciate is to pronounce words clearly and distinctly, the verbal sense of articulate.

clue.text: Car makes little progress on thoroughfare without one

definitions.note: loose: a con-rod is a car engine part that shuttles to and fro without going anywhere

indicators.note: without means lacking, so the word that follows loses the letter for one

parts.note: C is the opening letter of Car; how the setter means this letter to be taken is uncertain
taken as written
a road is a thoroughfare
a means one

explanation.surface: A car crawls along a road that is empty of other traffic.
explanation.walkthrough: This parse is uncertain. 'On thoroughfare without one' clearly gives ON and ROAD minus A; where C comes from and how the definition works are unclear, and only the crossings support the third letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A con-rod links piston to crankshaft, moving up and down endlessly while staying in place, so it makes little progress itself.

clue.text: Police do with riot, forming a ring?

indicators.note: to police something is to keep it in order, so these letters are put into a new order

parts.note: the first set of letters to be rearranged
the second set of letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Riot police form a ring around a crowd.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Police' and 'riot' look like a single phrase, riot police; 'Police' is the instruction and 'riot' is part of the material.
explanation.definitionFit: A toroid is a ring-shaped solid, like a doughnut, so the question mark flags an example.

clue.text: Tall wobbly antique, missing nothing (7, two words)

indicators.note: something wobbly is unsteady and out of true, so these letters are reordered

parts.note: taken as written
an antique thing is old

explanation.surface: An antique dealer notices that a tall, unsteady piece of furniture is complete, with no parts missing.
explanation.walkthrough: TALL and OLD are mixed to give ALL TOLD.
explanation.definitionFit: All told means counting everything, in total, so nothing has been left out of the reckoning.

clue.text: Piece of buhl, unarguably of old silver

indicators.note: a piece of something is a part of it, so the letters lie within the words

parts.note: the run of letters across the two words

explanation.surface: A piece of buhl furniture, inlaid with what is unarguably old silver.
explanation.walkthrough: Buhl is ornate inlay of brass and tortoiseshell. The alchemists linked silver with the moon.
explanation.definitionFit: In alchemy silver was ruled by the moon, so lunar was the old term for things of silver.

clue.text: Impressively good barley

parts.note: big can mean impressive or on a grand scale
G is the abbreviation for good

explanation.surface: A farmer praises a fine crop of barley.
explanation.walkthrough: BIG followed by G gives BIGG. 'Impressively good' looks like one phrase of praise, but it splits into two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Bigg is a hardy four-rowed variety of barley grown in Scotland and northern Britain.

clue.text: Chilled, like eels perhaps? Sounds like it

indicators.note: sounds like says the answer's pronunciation matches the phrase before it

parts.note: jellied eels are a traditional London dish

explanation.surface: Eels served cold from the fridge in a London pie shop.
explanation.walkthrough: Jellied eels are a traditional East London dish of chopped eel set in jelly.
explanation.definitionFit: Gelid means icy cold, so it describes something thoroughly chilled.

clue.text: This Gerard's a nuisance in bed, the lady's first therein

definitions.text: This Gerard's a nuisance in bed, the lady's first therein

parts.note: her is the possessive for a lady

indicators.note: first picks only the opening letter of the word it goes with

parts.note: the opening letter of bed

explanation.surface: A gardener complains that a weed named Gerard has invaded the flower bed.
explanation.walkthrough: Herb Gerard is ground elder, a notorious weed in garden beds. The parse of 'first therein' is not fully clear.
explanation.definitionFit: Herb Gerard, or ground elder, spreads relentlessly through flower beds and is a gardener's pest.

clue.text: Ray brought about maturity in millet

indicators.note: brought about means placed around, so the note wraps the other piece

parts.note: ray, or re, is the second note of the sol-fa scale
the age at which someone comes to maturity

explanation.surface: Some ray of sunshine has brought a millet crop to ripeness.
explanation.walkthrough: Ray is a sol-fa note here, not sunlight.
explanation.definitionFit: Ragee, also spelt ragi, is a cereal grass of India and Africa, a species of millet.

clue.text: 'No fuel rod that's faulty' rule applied to type of heating

indicators.note: applied to means stuck onto the end, so one piece is attached after the other
a faulty thing is not in order, so the quoted letters are rearranged

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged
R is the abbreviation for rule

explanation.surface: A safety rule for a nuclear plant forbids faulty fuel rods in the heating system.
explanation.definitionFit: Underfloor heating warms a room through pipes or cables laid beneath the floor surface.

clue.text: Ousel quitting fair feature of US boggy copse

indicators.note: something quitting leaves, so the named bird's letters are taken out

parts.note: a merry-go-round at a fair, spelt with a double R in American English
the bird's name, taken as written

explanation.surface: A blackbird abandons the fairground for a soggy American thicket.
explanation.walkthrough: An ousel is a blackbird. Taking OUSEL from the American spelling CARROUSEL leaves CARR; 'of US' belongs with the fair, not the copse.
explanation.definitionFit: A carr is fen woodland of alder or willow growing on waterlogged ground, a boggy wood.

clue.text: Accompaniments to a big spread, about 51

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the scrambled letters go round the number
spread means scattered out, so the preceding letters are rearranged

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged
LI is 51 in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: Side dishes laid out to go with a grand banquet for around fifty guests.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A big spread' reads as a feast, so 'Accompaniments' looks like side dishes; it is the musical sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Obligati is a plural of obligato, an instrumental part that accompanies a melody and must not be left out.

clue.text: Mountaineer's link, e.g. cork backing

indicators.note: backing means moving backwards, so the word is read from its end

parts.note: cork is the bark of the cork oak

explanation.surface: A climber's piece of kit, perhaps with a cork backing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Backing' looks like a lining for the link, but it tells us to reverse BARK.
explanation.definitionFit: A krab is a karabiner, the snap-link climbers use to clip the rope to their protection.

clue.text: A Greek township performed circuits wearing crowns

indicators.note: to make circuits is to go all the way round, so one piece encloses the others

parts.note: to perform something is to do it
a deme was a township or district of ancient Attica
taken as written

explanation.surface: In an ancient Greek town, crowned performers process around the streets.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Performed circuits' reads as laps of a track; 'circuits' is only the instruction to wrap.
explanation.definitionFit: Diademed means adorned with a diadem, a jewelled headband or crown.
